name: Amazon Aurora DSQL
tagline: Serverless, active-active distributed SQL on AWS with PostgreSQL compatibility and no instances to size.
description: Aurora DSQL is AWS's serverless distributed SQL database, generally available since May 2025. It splits query processing, transaction adjudication, journaling and storage into independently scaling services, uses optimistic concurrency with snapshot isolation, and can run as a multi-Region cluster where both Regions accept strongly consistent writes. It exposes a PostgreSQL-compatible interface with IAM-token authentication, though it supports a deliberately reduced feature set: no extensions, triggers or PL/pgSQL, and foreign keys and expression indexes only arrived in 2026. Pick it for new AWS-native OLTP services that want zero capacity planning and multi-Region writes; avoid it for lifted-and-shifted Postgres apps.

pricing.notes: First 100,000 DPUs and 1 GB of storage each month are free; no instance or capacity charges.

scale.notes: Reads, writes, compute and storage scale independently; clusters default to 10 TiB and can be raised to 256 TiB; multi-Region clusters pair two Regions with a witness Region.

strengths: No instances, ACUs or shards to manage; pay per DPU consumed
Multi-Region clusters with strongly consistent writes in both Regions
Optimistic concurrency avoids lock contention and scales reads and writes independently
IAM-based authentication and native connectors that refresh tokens automatically
Generous monthly free allowance for small workloads
weaknesses: Large Postgres feature gaps: no extensions, triggers, PL/pgSQL, sequences-heavy patterns or LISTEN/NOTIFY
Transaction limits on rows modified and duration require batching large writes
OCC conflicts surface as retries the application must handle
AWS-only and young, with a fast-changing compatibility matrix
useCases: New AWS-native microservices needing zero-ops relational storage
Multi-Region active-active user, order and entitlement data
Serverless apps on Lambda with spiky traffic
Ledgers and counters that must never lose a committed write
notIdealFor: Existing Postgres apps relying on extensions or stored procedures
Bulk ETL loads or long-running transactions
